newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Government fingered for dive in NZ confidence.
newsitem.headline: Government fingered for dive in NZ confidence.

text.p: The New Zealand government got the flak for two independent surveys published on Monday showing a dive in business confidence.
Apart from a trough caused by last year's pre-election nerves, confidence slumped to set a six-year low in April, according to National Bank of New Zealand's monthly survey.
And the independent New Zealand Institute of Economic Research (NZIER) said in its Quarterly Survey of business opinion that "positive signs of economic activity were few and far between".
NZIER argued the postponement of tax cuts intially planned for 1997 had quashed hopes of a consumption-led recovery.

The survey was the institute's first since the coalition government formed last December. One of thc centre-right administration's first acts was to postpone by a year a billion dollar tax cut package it had originally planned for July.

Treasurer Winston Peters said he was unrepentant for the impact of fiscal policies which include a controversial plan to boost public spending by NZ$5 billion (US$3.5 billion) over the next three years.
In comments to Radio New Zealand he sought to play down the confidence surveys, claiming they overstated key factors.

"They tell me (businesses) are concerned about the rise of the dollar... Well let's have some credit being given where it is due, the dollar has been arrested and since January has been stable. That's not been the pattern of the last three years."
Data showing March year underlying inflation at 2.0 percent was lower than predicted when the surveys were collated, he argued.
"Inflation is now dramatically down from those forecasts," Peters said.
Opposition Labour Party finance spokesman Michael Cullen jumped on the surveys, however, saying they showed that running a successful economy came down to more than "retail therapy".
"Our basic problem is an overvalued exchange rate which is knocking farmers, manufacturers and exporters while encouraging consumption and a current account deficit blowout," he said.

The National Bank's survey showed a net six percent of respondents anticipated general business conditions would deteriorate over the next year against a net six percent who believed the economy would improve in the March study.

The change in sentiment was reflected in lower profit, investment and employment expectations. Confidence was down in all sectors, but manufacturing took the biggest hit and was now the most pessimistic sector, it showed.
The surveys provoked mild responses in New Zealand's financial markets as shares took the gloom to heart while the debt market was inspired.

"Both the business confidence surveys out today, NZIER's and the National Bank's, were confirming a pretty soggy economy. So on the one hand you've got interest rates falling, and on the other you've got pretty lacklustre profit forecasts, and at the moment it seems that the latter's winning," said Don Turkington, Managing Director of brokerage Cavill White Securities.
The share market fell half a percentage point, with the NZSE-40 Capital Index down 11.05 points at 242.53 by 0230 GMT.
Meanwhile bank bill yields fell a hefty 14 basis points, with traders citing the surveys and a firm dollar as reasons.
Bankers Trust economist Nick Bennenbroek said BT still forecast a pick-up in economic growth.
"But the consitent trend of declining business and consumer confidence suggests this pick-up in growth could be delayed until late 1997."
Annual average GDP rose 2.9 percent in 1996 and most economists forecast growth of between 2.0 and 3.0 percent for 1997. (US$1=NZ$1.44)
